But, despite its misfires, Home remains a humorous and mythic romp.
Yet the play gains momentum as it goes on, thanks partly to the engaging commitment of the cast but also to Wiliams's skill with specifics: This play shines in the details.
Home proves thoroughly diverting in the hands of a memorably versatile three-member cast led by the outstanding Tory Kittles as Cephus.
Home is a fast-talking thrill of 90 minutes, bolstered by the breath support of the cast and the steerage of voice coach Kate Wilson.
With these three sublime performers on stage, the audience may never want to go home!
Home is a play meets lyrical ballad, where big themes—racism, resistance, identity, and, of course, home—are filtered through the trajectory of Cephus’ life, and the man
Home, directed in a most unassuming, unfussy way by Kenny Leon, is the most uplifting play to hit Broadway in a very long time.
Pugnacious in its own unique way, Williams’ odd positivity overwhelms history’s oppressive weight, making the denouement of Home seem possible.
These two women are nothing short of magnificent.
Real-world events have turned what I might have dismissed as a dated fable into what feels like a prescient reappraisal.
The production’s tone – especially as seen through Arnulfo Maldonado’s down-home set and Dede Ayite’s nostalgic costumes – is likewise consistent, if to a fault.

But since the aim of the ambiguity is to support diverse diasporic casting—something most audiences won’t experience unless they see What Became of Us twice—it’s a distancing decision that makes it harder to care about these characters.
The work is now receiving a Broadway revival by the Roundabout Theatre Company in which its charms prove much more elusive.
Home an enjoyable place to spend 90 minutes.
But rest assured Williams is smiling from above after every performance, for this atypical work is engrossing and entertaining.
This tale was the story of Cephus, and was told partially by him, and partially by two actresses who stepped into a variety of roles on his journey.
As Cephus, Tory Kittles shines brightly.
The story, cast, direction, and design are supremely expressive, entertaining, and affecting, and make Home a must-see show, so get your tickets while you can.
The ninety-minute play concludes with a glorious finale that crosses the finish line with pure genius, reminding us all that there’s no place like home.
And yet, by the time Home’s ending rolled around, I had succumbed once again to the old-fashioned pleasures of the play—and to its defiant optimism.

cn.t: Kenny Leon's well-acted revival of Samm-Art Williams' 1979 play earns praise for its poignant performances and poetic storytelling, though some critics find the material dated and the production uneven.

sg.vl: Intimate 740-seat house, center orchestra is the premium pick
sg.ra: Headout and TickPick both name center orchestra rows C-H (seats 105-109) as the best unobstructed views in the 740-seat house; rows E-J are called out as the value sweet spot before mezz overhang begins at row H. TripAdvisor reviewer: 'had great seats (row 3) ... seats further back would have been good too' given the small theater size.

sg.vl: Under deep mezz overhang, top of stage cut off
sg.ra: Headout guidance: 'Avoid the last three orchestra rows (N, O, and P) and the extreme corner seats.' Corroborated by search finding that beyond row N 'seats experience cut-off at the top of the stage' due to the mezzanine overhang that starts at row H.

sg.vl: Overhead sightline into the set, better-than-average legroom
sg.ra: Headout: 'Mezzanine seats as close to the middle of rows A to C as possible offer fantastic overhead views of the stage which are perfect for impressive sets and sweeping action.' Headout also notes 'better than average legroom, which makes up for the lack of inside aisles.' BWW forum poster recommended Mezz Row A seats 109-110 as a strong option.
sg.rr: A-G (single curved section, ~257 seats, no center aisle)

sg.vl: Budget-friendly with clean sightlines in a small house
sg.ra: Headout: 'rear mezzanine offers budget-friendly options with a pretty good view of the stage for a lower price.' TripAdvisor reviewer sat 'in the very last row of the balcony at this beautiful old theater and had an excellent view' — small-house intimacy holds up to the back wall.
sg.rr: D-G (within the single A-G mezz; back rows cited)

sg.vl: Heavily obstructed per TripAdvisor and BWW forum
sg.ra: TripAdvisor reviewer on house-wide sightlines: 'Most seats have excellent views of the stage, apart from the box seats labeled as obstructed view ... When this theater says obstructed, it means obstructed -- not partially obstructed.' BWW forum user tombomb31 on the box seats: 'I'm pretty sure I remember hearing they're incredibly obstructed.' Search notes: 'Anything that is on the far side of the stage you are sitting on is obstructed.'

vr.q: I definitely don't think that this is going to be a play for everyone because of the writing style and the narrations style. There were moments where I felt disengaged from material. For every moment that I felt disengaged, there was a moment that would bring me back in.
Overall I would recommend this play. I thought it was quite interesting, heartfelt, impressive but still in many ways simple and understated.
I ultimately really enjoyed the play... so go check out home it's a limited run at roundabout theater company and you will leave with your heart warmed
